endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: The HDO maintains an AI inventory of its AI solutions with a clear designation for each: opt-out eligible or not.

commentary.bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether consulting patient and family advisory councils improves the clarity or usefulness of AI disclosure materials, and no supplied study documents the hazard itself. The one endorsing source, a CHAI playbook, speaks to maintaining an AI inventory with opt-out designations rather than to advisory council review.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The recommendation rests on a single framework endorsement whose quoted text does not describe advisory council consultation.

The CHAI playbook language requires that a health delivery organization keep an AI inventory marking each tool as opt-out eligible or not. That provision supports disclosure infrastructure, but it does not state who should design or review patient-facing materials. The link between the endorsement and advisory council consultation is therefore indirect.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare AI disclosure materials developed with and without patient and family advisory council input, measuring patient comprehension, perceived usefulness, trust, and opt-out decisions. A descriptive study establishing how often patients find current AI disclosures unclear would also help confirm the hazard.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Advisory councils may not reflect these groups unless recruited deliberately, and any future evaluation would need to report council composition and test materials with these patients.
